title: Composition of functions
mini_lesson: On the workshop floor two automata are often coupled in a line, and the second one only ever works on what the first hands it. That chain is a **composition**: one function's output becomes the next function's input. Written $f(g(x))$, it is read from the inside out, so $g$ acts on $x$ and $f$ acts on whatever $g$ returns.

The same chain has a second name. $(f \circ g)(x)$ means exactly $f(g(x))$, and the circle is not a multiplication sign. The function written **first** is the one that acts **last**, because the other one is standing next to the input.

Swap the two machines and you have built a different machine. $(f \circ g)(x)$ and $(g \circ f)(x)$ almost never agree, because running a number through $g$ and then $f$ is not the same job as running it through $f$ and then $g$. Here **order is part of the answer**, not a detail of the writing.

You can compose without a number too. Wherever the outer function writes its input, write the **whole** inner function instead, brackets and all, then multiply out and collect. What comes back is a single function in its own right, and being able to build it is what later lets you test whether two functions undo each other.

steps: Read it from the inside out, so the $3$ goes into $g$ first.
The outer machine is handed that $5$ and nothing else: $f(5) = 5 \times 5 = 25$.

worked_examples.prompt: For $f(x) = 6x - 5$ and $g(x) = x + 8$, work out $(f \circ g)(2)$.
steps: The circle names the outer function first, so $(f \circ g)(2)$ is $f(g(2))$ and the $2$ goes into $g$.

worked_examples.prompt: For $f(x) = x + 1$ and $g(x) = 4x$, work out $(f \circ g)(3)$ and $(g \circ f)(3)$.
steps: For $(f \circ g)(3)$ the $3$ goes into $g$ first: $g(3) = 12$, and then $f(12) = 13$.
For $(g \circ f)(3)$ the $3$ goes into $f$ instead: $f(3) = 4$, and then $g(4) = 16$.
Same machines and the same input, and the answers are $13$ one way round and $16$ the other.

worked_examples.prompt: For $f(x) = x^{2} + 1$ and $g(x) = x - 2$, build $(f \circ g)(x)$ as a single rule.
steps: The outer rule squares its input and adds $1$, so the whole of $g$ goes where that input sits: $(x - 2)^{2} + 1$.
Multiply the bracket out in full: $(x - 2)^{2} = x^{2} - 4x + 4$.

cfu.prompt: Let $f(x) = 3x + 8$ and $g(x) = x^{2} - 4$. Evaluate $(f \circ g)(5)$. Enter one number.
cfu.hint: The circle notation names the outer function first, so $(f \circ g)(5)$ is $f(g(5))$: the $5$ goes into $g$, and $f$ never meets it. Work out $g(5)$ on its own and write it down as a single number before you touch $f$.
worked_solution: The circle notation names the outer function first, so $(f \circ g)(5)$ means $f(g(5))$: the $5$ goes into $g$, and $f$ acts only on what $g$ hands over.
Hand that value to the outer function: $f(21) = 3 \times 21 + 8 = 71$.
The other order would give $g(f(5)) = g(23) = 525$, so the two orders really are different questions.
